chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Dawud ibn Farqad, who said:

I heard a companion of ours asking Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the woman who dies with men, among whom there is no one with whom she can be married (non-mahram). Can they wash her while she is in her clothes? He (peace be upon him) said: 'Then that burden will be placed upon them, but they should wash her palms.'

key_terms.ذُو مَحْرَمٍ: A male relative with whom marriage is permanently forbidden
key_terms.يُغَسِّلُونَهَا: They wash her (ritual bathing of the deceased)

ai.seo_question: How is a deceased woman washed if only men are present?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of ghusl al-mayyit (washing the deceased) when mahram relatives are absent, establishing that men may wash a woman to avoid the sin of neglect, though full exposure is minimized by washing only the hands. It highlights the Shia scholarly principle of balancing ritual purity with modesty (haya), prioritizing the completion of the duty over ideal conditions. The ruling underscores the flexibility in gender interaction during funeral rites when necessity dictates.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ali Bin Al Nu’man, from Dawood Bin Farqad who said,

‘I heard a companion of ours asking Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about the woman who is dying with men, there not being among them one with sanctity (the one she cannot be married to). Can they wash her and upon her are her clothes?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘When that (situation) comes upon them, but they should be washing her palms’.
en.sarwar: 5. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Nu‘man from Dawud ibn Farqad who has said the following:

“I once heard a friend of ours ask abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about a woman who dies among men and none of them is of her relatives in that case can they give her Ghusl (bath) with her clothes on her. He (the Imam) said, ‘Thereby that feeling is apt to get in them, instead they must only wash her both palms (hands).”’
